Such is the spirit which seems to breathe over all its waters that I can well understand how the ancients worshipped their river gods. I regard the province of Quebec with all affection and would deny it no reasonable demand. I moved to the city of Toronto and have lived there for nearly thirty-five years. I know
The Address

the fair-mindedness of its people. I know there is no section which would seek to deny the province of Quebec anything it is entitled to. There might be a few persons of altered mentality who might desire to say something derogatory of the province of Quebec or of any other province but there is no section of the community in which I live, or of the province of Ontario as I know it, that would for one moment withhold from the province of Quebec anything that it is entitled to. On the other hand, I believe there is no important section of public opinion in the province of Quebec that would withhold from the province, of Ontario what it is entitled to.
But what do we find? We come to Ottawa and at first we find everything agreeable but before long within the precincts of this House we hear enunciated this idea of hatred. Mr. Speaker, it is the duty of members of this House, if they wish to serve the cause of their common Canadian patriotism, to see that an end is put to that kind of thing. As far as my race is concerned I am five generations Canadian. As regards my religion I will admit that I ought to have more of it but I am of a different creed from that declared by the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) this afternoon. If there are policies or principles or individuals to be attacked here let them be attacked and if they cannot defend themselves or give as good as they receive, let them suffer the consequences but surely attacks should not_ be made upon any part of tKe common patriotism of this country. Sir Wilfrid Laurier declared that love is better than hate. He sat for years in this House and knew the spirit that at times invaded it and in these words he has left his condemnation of that very spirit. I am willing to co-operate with other members of the House in doing my level best to see that the spirit complained of shall be forever exorcised.
There are rules of the House which are in the interest of decorum and the maintenance of the amenities of debate which require that no aspersion shall be cast by one member upon his fellow inembers. If a member offends in this particular, I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that we put him in a room by himself. This is merely an idea that I have in my own heart, and I say that no member should be permitted to speak disrespectfully of any province, or the people of any province as a whole. I submit if there was some amendment to the Rules of the House carrying into effect that idea, the legislation of this Fourteenth

parliament would advance the interests of this country beyond anything that we now imagine.
As far as I am concerned, let me say that I have no other interest than that of my country, Canada. My constituency is East Toronto. I know that it is a legal fiction that when a member is elected for a constituency he becomes, ipso facto, a representative of the whole country, and that he is not allowed to advance something which means the benefit of his own constituency or his own province, if it does not run on all fours with the betterment of the whole country. With that feeling, I want to say that I intend to attend the sessions of this House. I have no other occupation at the present time, and no business that calls me specially away from here prevents me giving my full attention to the sessions of this House. If any member of the House thinks that I, in my humble capacity, can do anything to advance the interests of any portion of this Dominion, or to improve the condition of the people of any part of Canada, I say right now as emphatically as I can, that I am at the service of that hon. gentleman. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that this unity, this prosperity which we are sure Canada is entitled to, and which the future will give it, can only be obtained if we, once and for all, really strive to become a united band, with no other object than the advancement of our country.

speakeroldname: Mr. E. J. SEXSMITH (Lennox and Addington) :
speechtext:
I wish, Mr. Speaker, to join with hon. gentleman in extending to you my sincere congratulations. I am not quite satisfied in my own mind as to the advisability of continuing this present discussion. I have been educated and entertained, and I might say that conscientious and constructive discussion may have a place yet in these proceedings. We are told that in a multitude of councillors there is safety. As one just undertaking the responsibilities of a member of this House, I do not intend to delay the proceedings by a long-drawn out speech. I desire, in a very humble way, to summarize some of the principal thoughts that have been expressed in relation to the Speech from the Throne. One hon. gentleman on this side of the House said that it was wise for us to consider the statements that were made in Parliament because they went out through the country. I believe he was right in the declaration, but the thought came to my mind: was it not just as important that this Parliament should

The Address
consider some of the statements that have been made and sent here from the country? I desire to state frankly that this Government is starting under very difficult circumstances, and an economic recovery cannot be brought about in a day, but it is my conviction that the Government will attain its objective, namely, the restoration of the political, economical and social life of Canada to a state of normality. What are some of the statements that come from the people of Canada to this Parliament? The people of Canada very emphatically stated on the 6th of December last that they wanted a change of government.
Hear, hear.

I do not believe in abusing the retiring government. I do not think that we get anywhere by abusing one another. Very definite statements have been made, that there was to be a revision of the tariff, that the railways should be owned and managed by the government, that the natural resources of the Dominion should be developed, and that constructive economy be practised in the administration of the country's affairs. Something has been said about unemployment. I will admit that the condition is very, very serious. But it is serious in the respect that it is an indication of a defect in administration. When these symptoms arise in Canada, it is time for statesmen and for everybody to begin and diagnose the case. Sir, I say that, while there have been worldwide conditions brought about by the Great War, and while there has been reaction resulting in pessimism, deflation in prices and so on, we believe that the national policy has outlived its day of intended usefulness. We are of the opinion that its continuance in force has been the underlying cause of Canada's present condition. We sometimes spend a good deal of time in swatting the fly, on account of the contagion that his little feet carry, forgetting to clean up the cesspools and the slough ponds that are the source of the trouble. We want revenue; of course we do. We lave a debt to pay. But a policy that brings in revenue and places a small percentage in the national treasury, allowing the major portion to find its way into the pockets of individuals, is destructive. The present high tariff is destroying the equilibrium of the nation, economically, financially and industrially. One of the main essentials of good statesmanship is the ability to strike and maintain a true balance in national affairs, but we believe that the present system is
submersive of the best interests of the country as a whole. What is the solution? It is to be found in a change of policy.
Something has been said about agriculture, and reference was made to the subject in the Speech from the Throne, in a faint, though judicious, way. I am sorry that the Progressive party is sometimes misunderstood. There seems to be a misunderstanding between the people of the rural districts and those of the -urban centres, not so much in the West, perhaps, as in the East and in Central Canada; but we trust that the day is not far distant when that misunderstanding will have disappeared. We do know that between the urban interest and the rural interest there is an interdependence; we know that those interests are positively inseparable; and we are also aware that a country must take care of its manufacturing interests. But there is another outstanding truth to be considered, and that is, that no nation that is over-industrialized is in a very normal condition. The greatest source of wealth to a nation lies in the fertility of its soil, and it matters not who tills that soil. If I understood the Minister of Justice (Sir Lomer Gouin) correctly, he said in his speech that the basic industry of Canada was agriculture. That being so, and statesmen having acknowledged the fact from time to time, we feel that agriculture should be encouraged, not, of course, in a selfish, narrow way, but having regard to its relation to other fundamental principles. Much has been said, by men who have pioneered the West and . who have laboured in this industry, as regards what should be done by governments. In summing up these opinions, we find that they want markets that are unbarred, they want economic transportation, and they want just remuneration, untampered with. Now, I believe that this Government will see to it that the agricultural industry receives fair treatment.
There is the problem of railways, and I do not think that the Minister of Railways (Mr. Kennedy) is to be envied. Indeed, I think it will devolve upon this House to assist him as best it can. This subject will be discussed by men who are eligible to deal with it. It pleases me to hear men, who have the ability and the experience, confining their remarks to this one particular question. We find that the railway freight rates are almost prohibiting transportation. In my own province it costs $500 to remove one hundred cords of
The Address

wood to a point about eighty miles distant from our county town. Under weak management the railways have perforce fallen into the possession of the Government. If there was anything on this earth that could die twice, I might say that we have been tariffed to death's door and have been railroaded nearly to the grave. There are two prominent factors in successful railway management-honest, competent direction, and the production of the natural resources of the country. I might place in the same category the three paramount problems, the railway problem, the immigration problem, and the problem of developing Canada's natural resources. These matters go together. Now, I do not wish to take up more time, because I do not feel that I have the ability to deal with these questions as they should be dealt with. But it is very necessary that something should be done, and we believe that it will be done.
I should like to say something in regard to the Soldiers' Settlement Board, which has been referred to rather cautiously. I believe that it is in the mind of the Government to do something more for our returned soldiers. Of course, much has been done; but we think that there could hardly be a limit to what Canada should do for those of her sons who fought her battle. Canada cannot afford to forget her returned heroes.
In conclusion, let me say that there are fundamental principles for us to consider. One has been mentioned by a number of hon. gentlemen, namely, unity; but I think that one of the main principles that should govern administration is unselfishness. When personal selfishness enters into the hearts of hon. members to whom the country entrusts the administration of its affairs, such selfishness is not only out of place, but is very destructive. Especially in all our deliberations I believe that we should be careful not to be biassed by racial or party prejudice, for it is only by maintaining a cool, dispassionate judgment that we can best advance the true interests of this great Dominion.

I did not intend, Mr. Speaker, to participate in this debate, but as several important points have been raised, and as some hon. members at least have expressed themselves as though inspired by rather a jealous feeling against my native city, I feel it incumbent upon me to address the House.

In the first place, Sir, I would crave the privilege of joining with those who have preceded me in conveying to you my most hearty congratulations on your election to the high position which this House has conferred upon you. I do that with all the more satisfaction because I recall that when I entered Parliament you were one of the first to extend to me that courtesy, friendliness and companionship which a new member very often so earnestly and keenly desires. Moreover, in view of all that has been said regarding the solid Liberal representation from the province of Quebec, I, as a Canadian, cannot be restrained from expressing my admiration at the rising to the position of First Commoner of this country of a Canadian from the old French province of Quebec who has been signally honoured by the great Republic of France in being permitted to wear in the lapel of his coat that, to a Frenchman, very cherished decoration of the Legion of Honour. I hope, Mr. Speaker, you will pardon me this personal reference. I speak it because I am more than ordinarily sincere and earnest in conveying to you my keen appreciation of your election.
Regarding the Speech from the Throne, which is the subject matter of this debate, it raises to my mind only three important points: First, the railways, next, the tariff, and, third, immigration. True, the Speech from the Throne makes reference to the recent election,-to the restoration of good times, so suddenly identified, which have come, according to the hon. leader of the Government (Mr. Mackenzie King) in response to the vindication of the principle that the people rule, while the old government, so full of wrong doing, has been thrown out, with the result that better times have dawned, like the rising sun on a new day, to warm and cheer every corner of this vast Dominion.
Now, when we commence to analyze the situation we need not be at all surprised. I for one was not in the least surprised at the result of the election. We but shared the fate that overtook practically every government of every other country that participated in the war. Our defeat was a natural consequence and a natural condition of the war. Would any man imagine for one moment that any government that had to undertake, with the energy, the force, and the perseverance which the Union Government and, later, the Meighen Government had to pursue, to tax the people, to raise enormous revenues, to restrict them in their liberties, to confiscate

The Address
their property, to compel in some instances enlistment and service for the defence of the Empire and civilization,-would any man imagine, I say, that that government was going to be popular with men who did not share the views of the great bulk of Canadians, and that those men were going to submit without venting their animosity upon what they conceived to be the authors of oppressive measures against themselves? People as a rule do not like to be taxed, when they are taxed they complain, and if they are taxed inordinately they rebel; which is exactly what has resulted in the defeat and overthrow of the Meighen Government. It has not been due to the lack of policy, to any wrong doing; it has simply been the natural and consequential result of the people objecting to pay the bill when the account is rendered. It is exactly the same as some people treat their doctor. They will call him out at night, they will plead on all fours for him to come speedily and often to their homes -"Don't neglect to call when you pass the door,"-but when he renders his account they will hardly know him as they pass him by on the street.
The political entity is practically the same as the individual, and I may tell hon. members of the Government that a day of reckoning will surely follow. They may take to themselves to-day the great consolation of having achieved victory. Well, I do not envy them their victory. It will be their privilege, their duty, their necessity to impose similar and even greater taxes, and to collect them, the burden is going to be grievously heavy, and the revulsion of feeling will speedily follow. When the tax collector comes for payment, the people will say, "Why this Government is no better than the other; we will have another change and see how it works."
Let us without bigotry approach and analyze the situation as far as we can. We have to-day a Government in power which has not the support of a majority of the members of this House. When the Government look across the floor and see ranged upon this side the Progressives and the old despised Tories, as they would feign make out we are, they must sometimes wonder as they go home at night how long the game is going to last and when the end will come. I hope they will have what the lion. Minister of Justice (Sir Lomer Gouin) promised to give the national railways-a fair trial. It would be the greatest possible misfortune to let them out of the hole they are in until they
have had a fair trial so the country will be able to pass judgment upon their acts. I for my part am not going to try to upset the Government,-just yet. I want to wait and see what they are going to do.
We have on this side a bunch of farmers. I remember when they started, I was in this House in the old time when we had the Union party and the Liberal party. Why, many of us who now sit in different places used to go to the same caucus,-the hon. member for Marquette was a member of the government then. Well, we had one or two hon. gentlemen who did not like their environment. They were very uncomfortable; they never loosened up as we felt they should; they were not as friendly as we thought they might be. They manifested a sort of narrow contractedness which did not come from us, and they began to edge off sideways. They did not know what they were, but they called themselves Farmers because most of them came from the West. In those days the hon. member who sat for the constituency of Red Deer, Mr. Michael Clark, was foremost in the expression of independent thought, although that independent thought did not, in most cases, appear to lead anywhere. But I believe he was at that time the right bower, if I may say so

the chief henchman-of the leader of the Progressive party, the hon. member for Marquette. The then member for Red Deer said: Well, as a name, "Farmer" will not do; " Agrarian " will not do, for it means the same thing if it means anything. So, if the people do not understand what Agrarian is we will call ourselves " Progressives", and it was Progressives from that day henceforth. Well, the late hon. member for Red Deer progressed to the very end. Finally he said: "There is nothing more to this. The Progressive party is simply a class; it represents nothing more than class selfishness. I cannot follow them in that line, so I will quit." And now we fail to see that distinguished and outstanding figure in this House. No longer do we hear the eloquence which had thrilled so many of us; no longer are we impressed with his whole-souled conviction of what must really be regarded as the Belial of absolute free trade.
Well, we must now designate our friends to my left as Progressives. But a rose by any other name will smell as sweet. I have listened very carefully to their addresses, and so far as I can gather it, their only text, their only idea, is the defence of the farmer. All they want is
The Address

to secure redress for the farmer; to see that he is accorded relief. They regard the farmer as the whole of Canada.
No, no.
No?
Open that other eye.

I want to remind my
hon. friend in all sincerity that there are other things in Canada besides farm labour and farm work.
Toronto, for instance.

Oh, you may sneer at Toronto if you like, but Toronto and Torontonians, I may tell my hon. friend, have just as much right to existence, despite his intimation to the contrary, as have the members from the Prairie provinces. And they too may need some things in order to enable them to enjoy independent life and to contribute their little mite to the progress of this country.
I am willing to grant all that can be granted for the benefit of the farmer; I am desirous of doing everything that is practicable in order to assist him. I am willing to listen to his grievances, and if any suggestion can be offered which would grant a measure of relief without ruin to the rest of the country, I for one should be prepared to support it.
I was pleased and edified, Mr. Speaker, by the deliverance of the hon. member for Marquette, leader of the Farmer party, in the early stages of this debate. I will at least pay him this compliment: he said in clear and definite terms what he really meant; his words seemed to carry with them his conviction; there was no humbug or camouflage about them. That went a long way with me, and I thought that if there was anything we could reasonably give him, it should be given. But there is a good deal that we cannot give him, as I see the situation. Let us take a look first at the railway problem. We have a tremendous mileage of railway in this country-twenty thousand odd miles, the result of long-continued maladministration. It does not make a particle of difference at whose door we lay the blame; the fact remains that we have a number of railways that have never paid, that are out of repair, and that cannot be operated without enormously increased expenditure for equipment and improvement of roadbed. I believe as firmly as any one in the nationalization of the railways and will go as far as I can toward carrying it into practical 
effect. I am with my hon. friends the Progressives heart and hand in the determination to hold what we have or what has been left for us to redeem in the pawnshop of the country. One hon. gentleman, speaking the other day, referred to the railway system as a miserable foundling. It is. It was conceived, I was going to say, in iniquity and born in corruption; it has marasmus of the very worst kind, and whether we can afford it relief or not I do not know. We suffered in this way. Year after year the railway corporations came to this House and received large subsidies which never went into the railways at all, but found their way into the pockets of the profiteers and mandarins who were using the railways as a means of milking not only the Dominion but the provinces as well; using them through the floating of bonds and the borrowing of money upon them. And would you be surprised to hear that for their venture they received a knighthood? Truly Canadians are a long-suffering people.
Well, now, what is to be the result? For some years to come, a decade at least, we shall have to provide $100,000,000 a year to keep up, to put in repair, to equip and operate these railroads and give them a chance to live. When you bring a starved infant to a doctor you are advised that if you want the child to have a chance for life, you will have to feed it. According to our information, and I believe it is correct, that is the condition our railroads are in to-day, and we have to feed them. Take the Canadian Northern; I would ask any man who goes over that road whether he imagines that in its present state it is a going concern? Not a bit of it. It will require improvement, repair, additions, new equipment, and so on. I venture the guess that we will have a deficit brought down close on to $100,000,000 if not more. If we are to maintain the policy of public ownership of railways we must not hesitate to face this condition; we must be prepared to meet it year after year. That is the first thing we have to think of.
In addition to that, we have to provide for the running expenses of the country. At the present time, to pay pensions and the liabilities contracted through the war, we have obligations amounting to $650,000,000 per annum. Our obligations have almost, if not entirely, doubled. The national debt of Canada steadily increased from the time of Confederation down to the beginning of the war, and it now represents a large an-

The Address
nual liability which my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) has to provide for in addition to other requirements. Is that a very engaging task for any hon. member when we have on this side, to my left, members clamouring for a lower tariff? Really what they are saying is: We want an abolition of the tariff, but we will be satisfied if you scale it away down. That, of course, would mean a depleted revenue from the tariff. If the Minister can meet their demands and the country's obligations I would like to see him do it. I doubt if there is a single man in this House or in this Parliament who is better qualified to speak on matters of finance than the present Minister of Finance, but I venture to tell him that it is absolutely impossible for him to meet the requirements for carrying on this country unless he maintains the revenue producing element which has entered into the policy of all governments in this country in the past. He may be able to obtain revenue by more taxes, but direct taxation is bad.
Now I come to the question of immigration, and it is a very important one. I am not one of those who are so keen to get immigrants into this country, because having lived in a large city all my life I have seen the evil results of immigration. We must hand-pick our immigrants in the future if we are going to develop. I have had a lot of trouble over this question of immigration, because I have a lot of Jews in my riding. However, to keep to the point, a man coming into this country who knows nothing about farming will make all sorts of promises to get into the country, and may say he is going on the land, but unless he has had experience in farming he ought not to be admitted as a farmer. In my judgment, we do not want immigrants who are going to infest our cities. How can we expect an inexperienced man to succeed as a farmer in the West, where, as the former member for Ped Deer used to tell us, the climate is so rigorous as to make that country a close cousin of the North Pole. He must be a sturdy immigrant to succeed in farming in our western country, and unless he is an experienced man with a great deal of energy and perseverance, after a while he will drift into the cities, walk around for some weeks looking for a job, and perhaps get work in some factory that he is not very well fitted for. All the time he runs great danger of joining the ranks of the unemployed, which means that he will have to be maintained and fed, and
that is what we in the cities particularly do not want. Let us help to keep the immigrants on the land. It is the -duty of this country and of this Government to offer every reasonable assistance to the immigrant to enabL him to stay on the land-and furnish him with the necessary opportunities that others have had who have preceded him and succeeded in farming. I would not be too keen to encourage even the artisan to come to Canada, but would rather encourage and lay the emphasis upon those who have had experience and training in the real science and practical art of agriculture.
Coming now to the question of the tariff, I am an adequate protectionist. What does that mean? It means that I am in favour of a tariff that is adequate to protect the growing industries that are springing up in this country. It is a tariff that must have the element of protection in it. One hon. gentleman to my left asked how the tariff could possibly help the farmer. Perhaps I may be permitted to answer that question. In the province of Ontario, farming is very different from what it is in the Prairie provinces, where the farmers have advantages which our Ontario farmers never had but would be delighted to have. The farmers in this province have not one-quarter of the advantages enjoyed by the farmers of the West.
Oh, oh.

Perhaps you think I
know nothing about it. I want to tell my hon. friends that I have worked on a farm in Ontario, and when we grew wheat we had to start in and cross-plough from the spring of the year till the next fall, and then start in again and break the ground and fallow it and rest it before we could get a crop of wheat, and then only a poor one. All that meant money. I was talking to a farmer from Manitoba some time ago, probably an exceptional one, and he told me of the conditions out there. He said, " My land is exceptionally good, I grant you. I have cropped wheat from my land continuously for thirty years, I have as good a crop now as I had when I started, and I do not fertilize at all." What Ontario farmer can say that? In Ontario the farmer has to alternate his crops, and fertilize continuously, and then he cannot grow wheat as the farmers in the West do. For him protection is his only salvation. Why? Because it builds up the industrial centres in Ontario, of which Toronto is
The Address

one, and furnishes him with a home market which consumes eighty-five per cent of all he produces. The Ontario farmer has to go into truck farming. That, of course, does not appeal to the farmer on the Prairie provinces, but it is a vital thing to the farmer in Ontario, and I am inclined to agree with the hon. member from British Columbia who said the other day that tariff requirements and tariff preferences are largely a matter of geographical location. They are fundamentally that. The hon. member for Yale (Mr. MacKelvie) told us in his speech the other evening that British Columbia needed protection because it was in close competition with the adjacent states of Washington and Oregon which, in some cases, produced better fruit, and therefore they needed protection to keep that fruit out. Some gentleman said "You should not have gone there" or words to that effect. Well if we followed that argument to its conclusion we might say with equal reason that the gentlemen who went to the Prairie provinces to grow wheat should not have gone there not because it was not good to go, not because the soil was not perhaps the best wheat growing soil in the whole world; but you were too far from the market and you should not have gone so far. The same argument will hold in this case; it is a matter of geographical advantages and requirements; and in this wide Dominion, stretching as it does from the Atlantic to the Pacific we must consider the conditions. It is all very well to talk about free trade in England but the conditions in Canada and the conditions in England are not parallel for a minute. We have a country to the south of us producing precisely what we produce, they are our competitors and we, to a certain extent, are theirs, they are producing grain and foodstuffs on certain parts of their soil that	are equal to
ours. They have been manufacturing with a great deal more speed and efficiency than we have yet been able to attain and the consequence is that in many instances, in many particular branches of industry, they have exhausted their raw material and they want the Canadian material to carry on their manufacturing. If we permit them to enter they will get our raw material, they will work it up into finished products, they will supply all our large centres, and they will then say "Well, the Canadian has not enough ingenuity to work up his raw material into finished products." You may say "Oh, but we will get the advantage, we 
will get cheaper goods." Yes, you may, those of you who live on farms of 1200 or 1500 acres in extent where wheat is produced and facilities given to ship it to market; but you must realize there are a large number of workers in the centres of population who are employed and gain their living by manufacturing those things which otherwise would be made in the United States at less cost and shipped in here at a cheaper price because over there owing to smaller overhead charges for manufacturing and the enormous numbers in their home market they can produce at far less cost for the Canadian market than we can do with our comparatively small population of eight millions of people. I can take you down to the lower end of New York city and to Jersey City, and through the state of New Jersey, and I can show you factories which are turning out clothing, ladies garments and various kinds of wearing apparel, which factories would sweep Canada and flood the whole of this Dominion with their surplus stock if it were not for the regulations which prevent the importation of such goods in enormous quantities into the Dominion. The tariff helps to keep these goods out and at the same time serves the good purpose of contributing to the revenue.
Some hon. MEMBERS Oh, oh.

However that may be as [DOT]you like. The Minister of Justice, I think, has declared what his policy is; he has declared for the Laurier-Fielding tariff. That was a protective tariff and that is the tariff which we in this corner of the House are going to support. While we are with you on the railway policy, on the question of public ownership, and will assist you sill we can, we are going to stand for adequate protection, which we will maintain, no matter how you may differ from us in opinion, is necessary and essential to protect industries in the large centres of this Dominion, and we hope we will convert you to our way of thinking.
A good deal has been said about differences of policy. I was somewhat surprised to read a new definition of Liberalism which was made by the Prime Minister in an address given in this city on or about the 13th of March last to the Liberal women of Ottawa. He defined Liberalism as an attitude of mind and heart; and I was wondering if it was possible to transform or change Liberalism as it used to be into this new doctrine, and whether that was henceforth to be its condition.

The Address
Some remarks were also made by the Prime Minister as to our being Tories. The leader of the House said that he never attempted to stretch Liberalism so as to embrace Toryism. Well I beg to remind hon. members that there are worse things than Toryism.
Some hon. MEMBERS What are they?

I want to tell my hon. friend (Mr. Mackenzie King) that if he reads history he will find that all the great efforts that have been made in this country, and a great deal of the prosperity and the progress which Canada has achieved, have been initiated, developed and carried to completion principally by the Liberal-Conservative party; and he can call them Tories if he likes. We are asked to-day to make concessions to the Northwest. Who made the Northwest?

The Tories.
Some hon. MEMBERSWe did.

I hear some hon. gentleman among the Progressives say "We did." The country was made before my hon. friends located there. It was a great Tory chieftain who initiated the building of the railroad that enabled my hon. friends to get there; they must not forget that the opening up of the West was largely due to Conservative efforts. When it came along to the time of Alexander Mackenzie, and I remember that time-the Dominion was practically on the rocks. Talk about farm produce and farming conditions! Why you could not sell anything on a farm anywhere. Potatoes were hawked from door to door in the city of Toronto for 25 cents a bag, and the vendor placed them in the cellar for that price too. It was the protective policy which resulted in the development of our industries, made possible the utilization and direction of our raw materials and enabled our home market to exist at all, it was that policy which gave confidence to the capitalist who put his money into the development of the manufacturing industries of this Dominion; and following this came the opening of mines and storehouses of treasure which are the astonishment of the world to-day and were never previously dreamed of. There is nothing becoming in the sneer sometimes indulged in on this subject by people who do not know the real, the fundamental and basic conditions on which this nation has been built. Then I want to say still further that it was the same party, in the main, who founded, fostered and developed
the British preference as against all other preferences.
That is a new doctrine.

That is something that is still in existence and will be carried on for a long time to come. We on this side are quite determined to wait and see. I am very keenly interested in the Budget which the Minister of Finance is going to bring down. I might venture to say, Mr. Speaker, that I really believe my hon. friends opposite are somewhat seized of the responsibility of their position because we do not hear so much from them this session; they are very silent, a contrast, as you will recall, Mr. Speaker, to their course last session. Why there was not a single debate at that time but we heard from them at length. For example there was the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon); we were certain to hear a blast or two from him and there were two or three others who were equally voluminous in their utterances and their menaces. Well, they are silent as the tomb. They are confronted to-day with a situation which must have astounded them when they realized their position, and probably they are cudgelling their brains to know what to do. It is our privilege to watch and wait.
I do not believe in long speeches. If a man cannot say all he has to say in thirty minutes, he had better leave the rest of his speech unsaid. May I say in conclusion, that I join with my hon. friends opposite, as I join with the party to my left, to work for the common good of Canada, for the development and prosperity of this Dominion, for the strengthening of the Empire as a commonwealth of nations, of which we form a part. We expect them to do their part and not to cast across the floor of this House intimations-I was going to say insinuations-of a sectional character, as if they were meant to taunt those of us who happen to hold opinions contrary to theirs. Such debates, and such distinguished characteristics of debate, cannot, in my humble judgment, contribute to the harmony and unity of purpose which should prevail in parliament. We hope that the result of our deliberations will be beneficial to all concerned, and I am sure this will be accomplished if we will only endeavour to yield a little, and if my Progressive friends will only realize that they cannot get everything they wish from Parliament. Rome was not built in a day,
The Address

and it will take time to accomplish results. I hope we will all work for the benefit of the country and the peace and prosperity which we hope to see this Dominion enjoy.

Mr. Speaker, it has been a great pleasure to me to meet face to face, many of the great men from the East whom I only knew previously by name. I congratulate you, Sir, on the high position to which you have been appointed. I have listened with some interest to lengthy speeches for a great many days during the recent debate. I congratulate the member for North Winnipeg (Mr. McMurray) on the splendid address he gave. It was very pleasing to most of us to find a young man holding, and giving expressions to, such high ideals. I have taken note of some of the passages-at-arms across the floor of the House, and truly on both sides it can be said that they did whet their tongues like swords and bend their bows to shoot their arrows, even bitter words. But, sitting here in my place listening, I wondered sometimes what they hoped to gain by it. However, I have obtained some information from these speeches. One thing is certain, that both parties, Liberal and Conservative alike, appear to gain inspiration mostly when they are slinging darts at each other.
I am pleased, Sir, with the fact that the Speech from the Throne deals very largely with those planks in the platform of the Farmers', or Progressive party which are most essential. Particularly does it mention the deplorable state of agriculture as regards markets and prices. That agriculture is in a deplorable state in Western Canada to-day is due to a variety of causes. One of these causes is the drought which has prevailed over very large areas of the Prairie provinces. I believe hail to some extent is responsible for hard times. But the worst feature, Sir, as regards agriculture to-day in Western Canada, and to a great extent in the older provinces as well, is the loss of faith and courage, and the dark outlook as to the future which is facing our people, brought about, not by natural causes, but by the persistent manipulation of legislation in the interests of those who control the manufacture and distribution of all our commodities, and who own and control all the facilities which we need to use in a public way. .
There are plenty of evidences to-day that agriculture is in a deplorable state in Western Canada. In support of that statement I point to the fact that some of our

rural telephone centrals are being closed at the present time, and some of the municipalities are also closing the day schools for the next six months, because the taxes cannot be collected. Mutual insurance companies are finding a hard time to exist, and some of them have already gone under. In every activity in which we engage at the present time, it is impossible to find a market at a price which leaves anything for the producer. In Saskatchewan, we have determined to follow diversified methods of farming and towards that end we have established a system of co-operative creameries. We are also engaged in the live stock business to an extent that does credit to that young province, but at the present time the markets for the products of the dairy are closed to us on account of high freight rates. The chairman of the Cooperative Creamery Company in Saskatchewan is authority for t'he statement that New Zealand is landing her butter on the coast of British Columbia cheaper than it can be shipped there from central Saskatchewan. The result is that butter cannot be produced and marketed except at a loss. Live stock cannot be moved under the present freight rates and leave anything for the farmer. Now that the prices of all farm products have fallen, in most cases below pre-war prices, it is only reasonable to expect that some consideration will be immediately shown in the matter of freight rates.
These things have darkened the outlook of the Canadian farmer, but the callousness of the late Government and the Railway Commission-place the blame where you like-will bring calamity, sudden and final, to the agricultural interests in Western Canada, unless something is immediately done to relieve the situation. The failure of the Railway Commission to lower the rates on grain before the last crop was moved, as we expected it would, has resulted in filching something like $18,000,000 from this already impoverished industry. We are still paying about $92 per car more than we should to get our wheat to Fort William. The effort to make the railways pay their way by repeatedly increasing the freight rates is only another case of killing the goose that lays the golden egg; it is curtailing production and providing less and less for the railways to earn. Surely it is only common sense to realize that freight rates in any country cannot be made higher than will permit commerce to move freely. Speaking of railways, I

The Address
claim there is only one policy to be followed if economies are to be effected, and that is a real system of consolidation of all government railways under one management and control.
I was very much struck with the speeches of two hon. members from the Maritime provinces. The member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) gave a long address relating particularly to the Intercolonial railway, but just what he wanted when he said that he did not want that road linked up with any other Canadian system I hardly know. Does he want that railway as a mere toy? The only grievance that I could find in his complaint was that the joy of free riding had been interfered with since the railway had been linked up with the Canadian system. 'Undoubtedly consolidation would be a benefit to all concerned in that there would be control in a centralized buying of rolling stock, motive power, rails and equipment of all kinds. There must also be union terminals and through traffic rates established before the railways can be economically run. At present the West provides an example in this respect of unified management and control. The Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Northern, -west of Winnipeg, have been incorporated into one system, and the whole of the West is reaping the benefit in service; and I can assure the House that we are proud of the railways in Western Canada, and the improvement that has been effected in the service since this was brought about, to say nothing of the economies.
Now, to enable the agriculturists to go on the land this spring with some degree of hope, faith, and courage, immediate and drastic measures are needed, particularly with regard to transportation and the marketing of our products. This is surely needed in the interests of the country as a whole, if the evil of the unemployment situation and trade depression is ever to be overcome. When you consider the fact that the western crop provides nearly 30 per cent of the value of all our exports, it is obvious that there is nothing that will restore confidence at one stroke, so to speak, so much as the re-establishment of the Wheat Board. It was a short-sighted policy on the part of the late government to discontinue this method of marketing our grain, just when the farmers of Western Canada began to have some faith in the work it was doing. It should have been continued at least during the whole
of the reconstruction period, which evidently has not yet passed.
Since our coming "to Ottawa it has cheered our hearts somewhat to find that the Government has taken note of the fact that our markets for some years past have been restricted; and we are glad that they are now setting themselves the task of obtaining freer trade relations with other countries, particularly the United States. Had I taken part in the flag-waving campaign of deception that was earried on in 1911, I should not be found as one of the number sitting under that banner to-day, knowing the awful consequences that have ensued.
Speaking of the tariff in general, it is in this system of trade prevention that we find the cause of the great loss in rural population in western Canada, particularly in the older provinces. We find in it, also the reason for the stagnation of development in the three prairie provinces and the older provinces as well. We see in this system of trade penalties the basis of that perfect organization in the Dominion to-day that controls all manufacturing and the distribution of every commodity which the workers on the land need to use. In the most stable part of Ontario there has been a large loss of rural population. Up to 1911 the rural population of Ontario, perhaps the banner province of the Dominion, had lost some 111,620 souls. I can point to some counties in that province to-day where great losses have occurred. For instance, the township of East Zorra in Oxford County has closed, during the last twenty years, 13 per cent of its farm homes, and Ashville, in Huron county, which I am informed is the finest agricultural township in Ontario, has closed 15 per cent of the farm homes during the same period. Surely there is a cause for all this.
While the Liberal government in years gone by was tardy in dealing with this great system of privilege, which robs the workers of their earnings and concentrates, under the control of the few, the wealth that is created, we are looking forward now with hope to something practical being done, and we trust that before the session comes to a close the Government will take itself seriously and try to implement the promises and pledges it gave in its platform of 1896, 1910-1911, again in the convention of 1919, and the promises it made during the last campaign that brought it into power. When the Minister of Justice (Sir Lomer Gouin) spoke the other day he said he believed in the Laurier-Fielding
The Address

tariff. I wondered just what he meant. It seems to me there are two phases to that tariff: one, as professed in their platforms and on the hustings during the campaign; the other, what they have actually put into practice. But at this time it is surely plain to all that the old national policy has had a fair trial and that after forty-three years of its operation under the most favourable circumstances conceivable it has brought about conditions that at the present time amount almost to a calamity. This old national policy, which my hon. friends to the right so strenuously uphold, was advocated for the purpose of looking after the working man. He was to have good wages, or as it was expressed, "a full dinner pail," and our natural resources were to be developed. What condition do we find to-day? That policy is responsible for the worst unemployment situation this country has ever faced, and has brought about the very calamities that it was intended to avert. It is no use saying that the war is responsible; the war simply put off the trouble for a time. Unemployment is rife from one end of the Dominion to the other, and, according to my hon. friend from Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth), while a quarter of a million men are idle, our manufacturers are importing raw material from any and every country where they can obtain it the cheapest, although our own mines and forests abound with the very raw material needed. What is the matter? I have it on the authority of the late president of the Massey-Harris Company that that company is dependent on foreign countries for seventy per cent of its raw materials. Our agricultural implement companies to-day import large quantities of Georgia pine for the tongues of their binders, drills, mowing machines, and other implements, while our forests abound with timber suitable for that purpose. The old national policy is a failure.

Will the hon. member
kindly tell us where the connection comes in between the national policy and the bringing of Georgia pine into this country to make tongues for binders and other agricultural implements?

I see the connection, Sir, in that the old national policy was advocated for the very reason that it was going to develop our natural resources. Those resources are still undeveloped, and our manufacturers are seeking their raw materials in foreign lands to-day.

I find on page 157 of the Report of the Dominions' Royal Commission that although Canada supplies over eighty-five per cent of the world's nickel, yet when that commission went through the Dominion only a short time ago there was not one nickel refinery in this country. I believe that under the pressure of war necessity some small refining plants have been established since then. I repeat, the old national policy has been a failure in that it has failed to do what it was advocated to do.
If trade had been carried on on a freer basis with the great country to the south of us, and with the rest of the world as well, we would to-day have a contented and virile population twice as large as we have now. Hon. members to my right have held up to us the benefits of the home market. I submit that a contented population upon the prairies to-day and throughout the other provinces would provide our manufacturers with a home market which their restrictive policy has destroyed. What folly it is to talk of a home market for the grain of Western Canada, three-quarters of which must be sold in foreign countries. That old theory has been exploded, and when it is put forth now we cannot treat it any more seriously than a joke. Freer trade relations will ensure wider markets. But then I am met with the question: What will you do for revenue, where is it to come from?
